$comment: Authoritative visual tokens (Constitution VII). Nothing in widget code may hard-code a
colour; if a value is needed and not here, the token is what gets added, not a literal.
M0 authors only the subset a list row needs. Later milestones extend this file rather
than starting a second one.
Light and dark are authored independently. Dark is NOT an inversion of light: inverted
greys go muddy in the mid-tones and inverted accents shift hue, which is why every
auto-darkened UI looks slightly wrong in a way nobody can point at.
Every pair in `contrast_pairs` is checked at build time by `cargo xtask contrast`, in
both themes. A failing pair fails the build.
$ramp_comment: Colour is authored in OKLCH and resolved to sRGB when this file is loaded. There is no
generated hex anywhere: `cargo xtask tokens` prints the resolved palette, but it prints
a *view*, and nothing has to be kept in sync with anything.
A ramp owns a hue, and nothing else does. That is the entire mechanism behind stable
greys: a token names a ramp and a lightness, so there is no per-token hue that can
drift. It could before. Measured, the previous hand-picked palette spread one grey
family across 264.5 to 285.8 degrees -- the light theme near 268, the dark SURFACES at
285.6 and the dark TEXT at 269-279. One theme held two different greys and the file
recorded no opinion about which was meant. The same amber token read 65.3 in light and
72.9 in dark, which is why an amber tuned in one theme looked slightly off in the other.
`l` is OKLCH lightness in PER-MILLE (974 is 0.974). An integer, because a file of
`0.974` is harder to scan and claims precision the eye cannot use.
Chroma has three spellings and each one is a different sentence:
omitted -- take the ramp's curve, chroma * (4*l*(1-l))^1.5. Only the neutral ramp
declares a curve. It vanishes at both ends because the gamut does (at
l = 1.0 the only colour is white) and because a grey wants its faint cast
in the mid-tones, not in the near-blacks where it reads as a cast.
`c`     -- absolute chroma. THIS MUCH COLOUR, whatever the gamut allows here. For
tints.
`s`     -- a fraction of the maximum in-gamut chroma at this lightness and hue. AS
COLOURFUL AS THIS HUE GETS HERE. For accents.
Both `c` and `s` are needed and neither subsumes the other, because sRGB is not a
cylinder -- the chroma ceiling at hue 260 is more than twice as high at l = 0.5 as at
l = 0.85. Only a matched `s` can mean 'equally saturated in both themes' when the two
themes place a token at different lightnesses; that is what fixes the accents, which
previously ranged from 0.785 to 1.05 of their ceilings (border/focus dark at 1.003 was
over the boundary, i.e. being clipped rather than chosen). And only a matched `c` keeps
a SUBTLE tint subtle, because a fixed fraction of a ceiling that varies fivefold does
not stay subtle -- see surface/row-selected, which is the token that proves it.
$type_comment: Type roles per UXDD 10.1. Five roles, each a size in logical pixels at the default
density plus an OpenType weight class.
Sizes are logical: they are multiplied by the device scale and the OS text-size
setting at use, never baked. Weight is a weight *class* (100..900), not a font file --
which face satisfies it is a platform question, and on Windows the answer is a
different font family per weight. See qs-text::fontdb.
Note that ui/sm and ui/md are both weight 400. The row's hierarchy comes from size and
colour, not from weight; using a heavier weight for filenames was considered and is not
what the UXDD specifies, because a dense list of semibold names reads as shouty.
$space_comment: Space and radius per UXDD 10.1. Both are in LOGICAL pixels and are multiplied by the
The space scale is a closed set of steps, not 'any multiple of 4'. A closed set is what
makes spacing decisions reviewable: 'why 14?' has no good answer, and the scale removes
the question by not offering 14. Column *widths* are deliberately not on this scale --
a column is sized by the content it must hold ("999.9 GB", a timestamp), which is a
measurement rather than a spacing decision.
Radius names the surface class rather than the number, so a row and a card cannot drift
$elevation_comment: How far a surface stands off the canvas, in LOGICAL pixels, as a closed set of named
steps like the space and radius scales -- a material names a step, never a number
The numbers are FUNCTIONAL, not aesthetic (research R7): looking straight down, a light
beside an element at the same elevation grazes its neighbours and contributes nothing
visible, so an emitter must stand ABOVE what it lights or its light never lands. That is
why `raised` (the selected row, the one emitter shipped so far) is four steps above `row`
rather than one: the gap is what its bounce crosses. `canvas` is zero by definition --
$focus_comment: UXDD 10.5: a 2px focus ring with a 1px contrasting outline, visible on every surface,
never suppressed. The outline is what makes the ring survive being drawn on a surface
close to its own colour -- a single-colour ring on a selected row can vanish, and a
focus indicator that disappears exactly when the row is active is worse than none.
$lighting_comment: Two halves under one key, and they answer different questions. `allowance` is what the
lighting pass may DO TO A SURFACE -- a contrast question, and gated. The rig (key light,
environment; tasks.md T010) is WHERE THE LIGHT IS -- an art-direction question, and not.
A value from one is never a valid answer for the other.
specs/002-ray-traced-mode/contracts/lit-contrast.md rule 3a. What the lighting pass may do
to each class of surface, per theme. Two classes, from rule 1a: a meaning-bearing element
may emit but must never receive, and the exclusion extends to the ground directly behind
it -- so a surface carrying a label takes almost nothing and one carrying none takes
everything. Which class a material is in is DERIVED from whether it declares `text`, never
declared, so a material cannot award itself an allowance.
Every number here is measured, by crates/qs-ui/examples/lit_probe.rs, and recorded in
research.md R13. Re-run the probe after touching any of them or any colour they apply to.
The asymmetry is real and is not a mistake in the file. A shadow darkens a ground, which
HELPS light-on-dark text and HURTS dark-on-light text; added light does the reverse. So the
dark theme's text grounds may go to full black and the light theme's may not go below
0.87, and that is the whole reason a single global range looked an order of magnitude too

$rig_comment: WHERE THE LIGHT IS (tasks.md T010). Not gated -- the allowance above is what the pass
may do to a surface; this is art direction. The two must not be confused.
Exposure is a MIX TOWARD A BOUND, never a multiplier (research R8, a mistake made
three times in this codebase before it became a rule). `key.share` is the key light's
fraction of a budget that sums to one; the environment gets the remainder. There is
no field that can push total exposure past the bound, which is the point.
`key.direction` points TOWARD the light, normalized at load, and doubles as the
reduced-motion RESTING POSITION (FR-029): under Reduce Motion every light sits at
exactly its authored value -- the key light here, the focus lamp at the focused
element itself, which is a layout fact and not a token. `key.size_deg` is the
light's angular size; it is what makes shadows soften with distance, and a light
with no size casts the hard offset shadow the feature exists to replace.
The environment's two stops are TOKEN NAMES, so the room changes with the theme
instead of being one room both themes have to share.

$comment: EXACTLY qs_gpu::frame::LIGHT_DIR, and a test holds the two equal. The PBR
bevels, the contact-shadow offsets and the raymarched shadows must agree
about where the light is, or the window's shadows point two ways at once
in a way nobody can name. The constant is the shader's copy; this is the
authored source, and they may only move together.
THE FOCUS LAMP (tasks.md T064). Keyboard focus is a light, so the shadows in
the window lean away from wherever it is. No direction, because a positional
light has none; no position, because that is a layout fact; no colour, because
this lamp contributes ATTENUATION only and attenuation is a colourless multiply.
`share` is the lamp's fraction of the shading budget directly beneath it, falling
off with distance. Like `key.share` it is a MIX TOWARD A BOUND (research R8): at
0.0 the pass is arithmetically today's, and there is no value that darkens a frame.
Both shading terms are in 0..=1 and the mix is convex, so the lamp can LIFT a
shadow the key light cast -- which is how focus becomes visible -- and can never
push a surface past its unlit colour. That is why nothing in the contrast gate
moves for this: the gate's worst case is the allowance floor, and a lamp only
ever works away from it.
`ambient` is the half a person actually sees, and it was added after LOOKING. With
`share` alone the lamp was measured at a peak of 7/255 and a mean of 3/255 across a
1200x700 window with focus moved eight rows -- arithmetically present, perceptually
absent. `share` only changes a pixel where the two lights DISAGREE, and a list of rows
at one elevation gives them almost nothing to disagree about. `ambient` dims the room
with distance from the lamp instead, which is what makes focus lit rather than merely
differently-shadowed. 0.18 leaves the far rows at 0.82 of their colour in the dark
theme -- well above the 0.55 the allowance would permit. A vignette that followed the
keyboard at full allowance would be the mode making the product WORSE, which is what
SC-012 exists to catch and what no amount of looking impressive should buy.
`size_deg` is roughly four times the key light's. A lamp hanging fourteen pixels
over a row is physically a broad source; a small one casts a hard second shadow
that reads as a rendering fault rather than as light.
FR-029 is answered by the lamp not travelling under Reduce Motion rather than by
a resting position authored here -- it rests AT the focused row, which is a place
the layout chose and not wherever an interrupted animation stopped.

$allowance_note: The dark theme's text grounds were allowed to go to FULL BLACK (R13 measured it as
free, because a shadow only helps light-on-dark text). The lamp made that unaffordable:
an emitting row's ground now runs from shadowed to lit, and no single ink survives a
range that reaches black at one end and accent-bright at the other -- measured at
1.04:1 for the dark ink against a fully shadowed row. 0.55 is the floor that lets one
ink cover the whole range; it costs shadow depth on surfaces that carry text, which
were producing hairlines anyway, and costs the CANVAS nothing because a receiver keeps
its own allowance. Re-run `lit_probe` before moving it again.

$substance_comment: What a file's facts make its surface out of. crates/qs-ui/src/substance.rs.
A material changes how a surface RESPONDS to light, not how bright it is, so none of
this is charged against the lighting allowance above and `cargo xtask contrast` must
report the same number with these values as with all three flat. A contrast failure
here means an encoding leaked into brightness, which is the one way this can be wrong
in a way a screenshot would not show.
ONE encoding, out of the four proposed. The premise above is only true for
EDGE-LOCALISED properties, and finding out which ones took rendering them:
size        KEPT. `bevel_normal` perturbs the normal only within `bevel` of the edge,
so while 2 x bevel < row_height the row's CENTRE -- where the label is --
shades pixel-identically whatever the file's size. Same argument
Material::composites already makes for Stroke and Rim.
age         DROPPED. Roughness feeds the GGX distribution, the Smith visibility term
and the Fresnel-roughness environment lobe, all of which change how much
light the WHOLE surface returns, under the label included -- and the gate
checks the albedo, so it cannot see any of it.
kind        DROPPED. Metal in a dark room is dark, not fixable inside the BRDF, and
kind already has two carriers (the icon and the extension ribbon).
permission  DROPPED. `env` is not reflectivity -- it is the key-light-versus-sky MIX,
so env = 0 is a surface lit entirely by the key light and it rendered
BRIGHTER, not duller. It is a property of the rig, not of the material.
Age, kind and permission all still reach the user in words: the modified and size
columns, and the per-row a11y description.
`span` is an EXPONENT here: 2^30 bytes = 1 GB sits at at_max. Logarithmic because file
sizes are; a linear ramp puts every ordinary file at the bottom and one video at the top.
at_max is capped by `the_bevel_stays_an_edge_treatment_at_every_shipped_row_height`.
Set at_min == at_max to switch the idea off; that is also what a token file with no
`substance` block gets.
$emissive_comment: LIGHT, NOT PAINT. This block is deliberately NOT inside `tokens`, and that placement is
the entire safety rather than a filing preference.
`Tokens::bloom_ceiling` is a fold over every entry in `tokens`: a pixel blooms when it is
brighter than every colour this palette can name. An emissive placed in `tokens` would
therefore raise the ceiling to exactly its own luminance, and a value is not greater than
itself -- so the bloom would stay off with a source authored, present and drawn. Keeping
it out here means the ceiling cannot rise to meet it, `Tokens::color` cannot reach it (so
no call site can paint a fill or set a glyph in it by typo), and there is no `role`,
because an emissive belongs on neither side of a contrast pair.
WHERE IT MAY BE SPENT is refused at load time rather than reviewed: only on a layer that
declares an `edge`. That is the band geometry `Material::composites` already excludes,
which makes it the one colour in the window no text is ever read against. Naming an
emissive in a material's `text`, `text_lit` or `over` is an error.
WHAT THE THRESHOLD STILL CANNOT SEE: the bright pass selects by luminance and has no idea
where the light it selects LANDS. `lighting.allowance.text_ground.addition_max` is 0.0 in
both themes, and no token file can check that. `cargo run --release -p qs -- --bloom-reach`

emissive/sweep-peak.description: The bright point travelling along the command bar's hairline, and the only thing in the window the bloom's bright pass can select. ONE VALUE, TWO ANSWERS, AND NO CODE BRANCHES ON THE THEME: it resolves to relative luminance 1.0, which is above the dark theme's 0.8986 ink ceiling and therefore light, and NOT above the light theme's ceiling of 1.0 -- several light-theme tokens resolve to white -- and therefore not light there. So the light theme shows no bloom and pays for no passes, derived by the fold in `Tokens::has_bloom_source` rather than stated anywhere. That is research R13's finding arriving from a third direction: the light theme has no emitter, because its page is already the brightest thing in it. IT IS WHITE, AND THAT WAS MEASURED RATHER THAN CHOSEN. l=980 s=1.0 was authored first, because the intent was an accent cast rather than a white flash: it resolves to rgb(0.960, 0.975, 1.000) at luminance 0.9414, clearing the ceiling by 0.0428 on paper. Drawn, it does not clear it at all. A one-logical-pixel band composited over the bar arrives at a CONSTANT 0.9387 of its authored luminance -- `--bloom-reach` reported 0 of 1,440,000 px with the source present, authored and above the ceiling -- so the real requirement is authored > 0.9573 and the accent ramp has nothing there. It has nothing anywhere near there: the gamut's chroma ceiling at l=1000 is zero, so the top of the ramp is exactly white at every `s`, and the brightest value that carries any cast at all is the one that fails. `s` is kept at 1.0 rather than dropped, so that a future band with full coverage picks up the cast this one cannot afford. THE ATTENUATION IS THE NUMBER TO KNOW BEFORE MOVING EITHER END: thicken the band and the factor rises toward 1.0, dim the emissive and the bloom silently switches off with a source still drawn.

surface/row-alt.description: Alternating row banding. Deliberately near-invisible: strong zebra striping competes with selection for the same visual channel.

surface/row-hover.description: Pointer hover. The four surfaces step by a uniform 26 per-mille of lightness in both themes, which is a perceptually equal step because that is what OKLCH lightness is for. The dark theme did not step uniformly before -- it went 224, 246, 288, 312 -- so hover was a bigger jump than banding by almost twice.

surface/row-selected.description: Selected row fill, and the NEAR stop of the selection ramp. Kept light enough that secondary and tertiary text still clear 4.5:1 on top of it -- selection must not degrade legibility. THIS is the token that needs absolute `c` rather than `s`: in the light theme selection is separated from hover almost entirely by chroma, their lightnesses differing by 5 per-mille, so expressing it as a fraction of the ceiling collapses it to c=0.008 and a selected row becomes indistinguishable from a hovered one. Every contrast check stays green through that, because contrast is a luminance ratio and cannot see chroma at all.

surface/overlay.description: Diagnostics overlay backing, and the DEEP stop of the command bar's gradient. Deep rather than near because the dark theme puts it at l = 0 and there is nothing below black to ramp toward.

surface/overlay-lift.description: The LIT stop of the command bar's gradient, at its top edge, ramping down to surface/overlay at the hairline. It is the WORSE of the two stops for every foreground on the bar â€” the ink is near-white, so the lighter end is the lower contrast â€” and is therefore the stop the pairs are declared against. The two themes need different lifts and that is not an oversight: a per-mille of OKLCH lightness is not a fixed number of 8-bit levels. 70 per-mille was used in both at first; against the light theme's l = 175 it reads clearly, and against the dark theme's l = 0 it spans about eleven levels of 255 and the ramp was indistinguishable from the flat fill it replaced. Only looking at it found that â€” every gate was green. 150 in the dark theme restores the same apparent lift.

field/one.description: The first centre of the ambient field behind the window. The four field tokens are the only coloured GROUNDS in the palette, and their lightnesses are chosen inside the interval the four neutral surfaces already occupy -- 948..1000 in the light theme, 224..276 in the dark -- for the reason the canvas sweep was: a colour that moves within an interval the gate has already blessed is affordable, and one that leaves it has to be paid for in text contrast. What varies between them is HUE, which relative luminance cannot see at all, so the field can be genuinely coloured while costing the ink nothing. The chroma is roughly twice as high in the dark theme because the OKLCH ceiling is not symmetric and equal absolute chroma reads as less colour on a dark ground.

field/two.description: The second centre. Amber against field/one's accent, because two centres a few degrees apart on the hue wheel blend into one wash and the point of a field is that the window has more than one temperature in it.

field/three.description: The third centre. The coolest of the four and the faintest, so the bottom-left of the window recedes rather than competing with the accent at the top.

field/four.description: The fourth centre, and the deepest: it sits at the bottom-right, where the window is furthest from the command bar the light comes from. It is the darkest ground in the light theme and the lightest in the dark one, which is the same direction -- away from the base -- and is why it is the centre the contrast gate has the least slack on.

shadow/contact.description: What a surface that sits ABOVE the ground casts onto it. The one token that is dark in BOTH themes, which is why it needed to exist rather than borrowing an existing one: a shadow is an absence of light, and absence does not invert with the theme the way a surface or an ink does. Every candidate already in the file is wrong in exactly that way -- content/primary is dark in the light theme and near-white in the dark one, so a shadow made from it would glow. It is not pure black in the light theme either: a shadow on a near-white ground is a soft grey, and full black reads as a hole cut in the page. It carries a trace of the neutral ramp's chroma so it sits in the same colour family as everything it falls on. Used at low opacity, always through a layer with an `offset`, so the shadow falls where the key light says it should rather than ringing the shape.

content/tertiary.description: Kind column and placeholder text. The lowest-emphasis text that still has to be readable on every row background.

content/on-lit.description: Lettering on a surface that is EMITTING. A lamp is bright in both themes, so this is dark in both -- the one token in the file whose value does not follow the theme, because what it sits on does not either. It exists because an emissive row changes the ground under its own label: the ink that reads on the unlit row is washed out on the lit one, measured at 1.53:1 before this token existed. `Material::text_lit` is how a material asks for it, and the contrast gate checks it against the material's LIT composite -- albedo plus the emission's closed-form peak -- so a brighter lamp is a red build rather than an unreadable filename.
content/on-lit.$measured: At row/selected's authored emission the lit ground peaks near l=760 equivalent; l=180 clears 4.5:1 against it with room for the lamp to be turned up.

content/on-overlay-dim.description: Lower-emphasis text on an overlay backing: the command bar's Back/Up chips, its separators, and every breadcrumb segment that is not the open folder. Exists because the bar was borrowing content/tertiary, which is authored for the ROW surfaces â€” light in the light theme â€” and the bar is dark in both. Nothing caught it because no contrast pair covered that combination; declaring the gradient's stops did, at 3.12:1 against a 4.5:1 requirement. Same stop in both themes, for the same reason content/on-overlay is: the backing is dark either way.

content/on-overlay.description: Text on the diagnostics overlay. Identical in both themes -- the overlay backing is dark either way. Identical is now literally the same stop rather than the same hex repeated.

border/subtle.description: Row separators and column rules. DECORATIVE: not in contrast_pairs, see the note there.

border/focus.description: Keyboard focus ring. Meaningful, and gated. Matched `s` is what makes the two themes equally saturated: the ceiling at l=505 is 0.206 and at l=753 it is only 0.127, so equal absolute chroma was never available. The dark ring previously sat at 1.003 of its ceiling -- outside the gamut, being clipped -- and 0.95 puts both rings just inside it.

border/focus-outline.description: The 1px hairline outside the focus ring (UXDD 10.5). Opposite polarity to the ring so the pair stays visible on any surface, including one whose colour is close to the ring's.

icon/badge.description: The extension badge's chip (UXDD 10.4). Reverse polarity: dark on the light theme, light on the dark one. surface/overlay was tried first and is wrong â€” it is #000000 in the dark theme against a #1b1b1f surface, so the chip vanished and the extension read as text floating under the icon. A chip is only a chip if it has an edge against what it sits on, which is why this is gated against all four row surfaces rather than only against its own text.

icon/badge-text.description: The extension inside icon/badge. Its own token rather than a borrowed one: the chip inverts with the theme, so the text has to invert with it, and no existing foreground does.

icon/folder.description: The folder icon's tint (UXDD 10.4). Amber rather than the accent blue for two reasons: a folder is warm in every shell a user has ever used, and a blue folder sitting inside a blue focus ring made the ring harder to see on the one row that most needs it. `role` is border because a filled icon is a non-text graphic held to WCAG 1.4.11's 3:1, not to a text ratio.

rail/conflict.description: Status rail: conflicted. All four status-and-icon colours share one `s` of 0.9, so they are equally saturated as each other and across both themes -- which they were not: measured against their own ceilings they ran 0.785 to 1.05.

content/on-accent.description: Lettering on an ACCENT-coloured surface, in both themes, because an accent surface is saturated in both. It arrived with the lamp: once row/selected's albedo became the light's own colour -- the only way `shade_pbr`'s `albedo * emission` can emit light-coloured light rather than a brighter version of a grey -- the row became a blue panel in both themes and the ordinary row inks stopped working on it, measured at 1.23:1 for content/secondary in the light theme. This is the standard selected-row pairing every platform ships, arrived at from the lighting rather than from fashion.

surface/raised.description: The panel a popover or the inspector sits on: the opaque form of `chrome/popover`, and the floor UXDD 10.7 chose for backdrop blur before the effect existed. Named by that table and absent from this file until prim-backdrop-blur needed it, which is the order the section asks for -- the fallback is a design decision made in advance, not a residue of what the effect degraded to. In the LIGHT theme it is l = 1000, the same as surface/base: the canvas is a field whose centres sit in 948..1000, so a white panel is already brighter than everything around it and there is nothing above white to reach for. Separation there comes from the border and the elevation, not from lightness. In the DARK theme it is l = 288, above the list's 224 and its alternate's 250 so a panel reads as being in front, and below border/subtle's 302 so the panel's own edge is still visible against it.

$material_comment: A material is a named LOOK: a stack of effect layers, each naming a PrimKind the
pipeline can draw plus the tokens and scale steps it is made of. `Tokens::paint` is the
only way a surface asks for one, and after the conversion there is no second place that
decides what a selected row looks like -- which is the whole value, not the shorter call.
Every value here is already a token: a colour name, a step from the space scale, a radius
class. `reach` is a space step because a halo's reach is a spacing-scale distance like
every other gap in a row. `angle` is in degrees, measured the way the surface's
coordinates run: 0 ramps left to right, 90 top to bottom. `width` and `thickness` are in
logical pixels, because there is no width scale -- `focus` above states its two the same
way.
`flat` is what a ramp becomes when effects are switched off, and it is stated rather than
conventional: the command bar's resting colour is its FAR stop and the selection's is its
NEAR one, so any rule that picked for the author would be wrong for one of them, and
wrong in forced-colours mode, which is the mode with the least slack.
`over` and `text` are what the contrast gate reads, and they are the reason a material is
worth more than a helper. A declared pair asks whether a foreground is legible on a
token. A material asks the question text actually faces: is it legible on whatever the
layer stack COMPOSITED to. Those differ whenever a look is more than one flat fill, and
the second catches things the first cannot -- a halo moved above the fill it belongs
under changes no token at all, and every declared pair would stay green while the
secondary and tertiary text quietly lost the 4.5:1 their token is authored to preserve.
Each material contributes text x over x composites, and the composites are the product of
its layers' in-shape stops, so a two-stop ramp is checked at BOTH ends.
Strokes and edge bands are deliberately not composited: a rim and a one-pixel hairline
are not backgrounds anything is read on, and gating text against them would refuse looks
that are perfectly legible.
A ROW IS THE WRONG SHAPE FOR A SUBTLE RAMP, and that is the finding this block exists to
keep. row/hover and row/selected were both authored as gradients -- a top-lit hover and a
selection dissolving across the row -- and `cargo run -p qs-ui --example material_strip`
showed why neither survives. A row's ramp is constrained at BOTH ends by the three
content roles that have to clear 4.5:1 on it, which leaves an interval of about 26
per-mille; in the dark theme that is two or three 8-bit levels, so the hover ramp was
indistinguishable from the flat fill it replaced, and the selection's horizontal ramp
crossed its four levels as four hard vertical edges the full height of the row. Both
gates were green through it, in both themes, because a contrast ratio is a property of
the endpoints and says nothing about what happens between them.
The bar and the shelf keep their ramps and read correctly, and the difference is
geometry rather than luck: they span an interval three times wider (surface/overlay to
surface/overlay-lift is unconstrained at the deep end) across forty pixels rather than
twenty-eight, so the same quantization lands as a step every two pixels instead of every
ninety. The rule to carry forward is that a ramp needs enough 8-BIT LEVELS to be smooth
and enough PIXELS to spread them over, and a token file records neither.
This is the same failure surface/overlay-lift already records one paragraph up. It has
now happened twice, and both times every automated check stayed green.

surface/canvas.description: The list's ground, and the biggest surface in the window. It was the draw list's CLEAR COLOUR and nothing else -- one flat value across seventy per cent of the screen, which is what made a window full of carefully lit rows still read as unfinished. It is now a FIELD: four coloured centres drifting behind everything, and the ONLY coloured grounds in the palette. The field replaced a top-to-bottom gradient rather than stacking on it, for two reasons that agreed. The first is composition: a field's ground is opaque, so a field drawn OVER a ramp erases it, and a field drawn UNDER an opaque ramp is erased by it -- three full-viewport layers was never two pictures plus a third, it was whichever one was last. The second is that the ramp's job is inside the field's: the two upper centres sit close to surface/base and the two lower ones further from it, so the window still deepens away from the command bar and the light still has a direction. What is new is that the direction now has TEMPERATURE -- accent at the top left, amber at the top right, green and a deeper accent below -- which is the thing a two-stop ramp of one hue could not say at any subtlety. Over it is the conic SWEEP, translucent, travelling one turn per cycle. Colour costs the text nothing here and that is by construction rather than by luck: every centre's lightness is inside the interval the four neutral surfaces already occupy (948..1000 light, 224..276 dark), and relative luminance cannot see hue at all, so the field is genuinely coloured and the gate's answer is the one it already gave about those surfaces. The gate checks each centre at the full amplitude, not the field's average -- an average is a colour that exists nowhere in the window. The dither is what lets it be this subtle: a handful of 8-bit levels spread across a whole window bands without it, which is the failure surface/overlay-lift and the row wash both already recorded, and at this size it would be the most visible artefact in the application. Amplitude is 0.6 because this is ground: a ground that competes with the list has taken the list's job. The field and the sweep both drift only while some other animation is holding the frame loop awake, so the window breathes during a scroll or a navigation and is a still picture in between -- which is what keeps SC-003 structural rather than careful.

row/body.description: The row's own body, on the even rows. It exists so that a row is a SURFACE rather than a region of the canvas, and so that crates/qs-ui/src/substance.rs has something to vary: roughness carries time since modified, the bevel carries size, the environment carries permission. It is TRANSLUCENT, and that is the correction to a mistake worth recording. It was opaque, and its albedo was exactly surface/base -- which was defensible while the window's ground was also surface/base, and became wrong the moment the ground became a drifting colour field: rows tile the entire list area, so an opaque row body painted over every pixel of that field and the ambient ground was invisible in the running application while looking perfect in the material harness, which draws four rows and leaves most of the canvas showing. At 0.34 the field is the window's ground again and a row is a lit surface sitting ON it. The zebra banding is a third of what it was as a direct consequence, which the palette already wanted near-invisible. What the translucency does NOT do is let a fact leak into brightness: substance still touches only the bevel, and the_row_body_composites_to_exactly_the_colour_it_replaced now measures the invariant that matters -- the composite introduces no third colour, it lies on the line between the ground and the declared albedo at one mixing fraction shared by every channel. Every field centre is in `over`, so the contrast gate checks the label against the ground it actually has rather than against the one it used to have. The CPU floor is the albedo, so the fallback tier draws the flat ground it always drew.

row/body-alt.description: row/body on the banded rows, and the ONLY difference is the albedo. Two materials rather than one painted in two colours because a material owns its colour -- that is what keeps row/selected and row/hover exactly coincident -- and the alternative, letting a call site pass a tint, is the second place that decides what a row looks like. Translucent at the same 0.34 as row/body and for the same reason: see that material's note on why an opaque row body made the ambient field invisible in the real application.

row/hover.description: Pointer hover, and press, which is the same wash layered a second time so a press deepens whatever is beneath it rather than arriving as a second colour. It was authored as a top-lit ramp and is flat again, because looking at it settled the question the numbers could not: see $material_comment on why a row is the wrong shape for a subtle ramp.

row/selected.description: A selected row, and the one surface in the window that is a LIGHT SOURCE rather than a thing that is lit. It used to be a halo, a fill and a rim, and it read as a 2015 box-shadow for a reason that was structural rather than a bad number: a glow and a rim are both functions of |SDF distance| and nothing else, so neither contains a light direction, a scene or a neighbour, and no amount of tuning makes a symmetric ring around a rectangle look lit. The order is inverted now. The Pbr surface EMITS along its bevel -- contract rule 1a names selection state a source that may emit -- so the light comes from the row's own edge, and the halo above it is the spill from that edge rather than the main event, at less than half its old opacity. Beneath everything is the CONTACT SHADOW: the same shape, dark, tight, displaced two logical pixels along the direction the key light says a shadow falls. That single layer is most of why the row now reads as an object above the ground instead of a rectangle printed on it, and it is the thing no combination of the old three could express, because a material had no way to displace a layer until `offset` existed. None of this costs the text anything, and that is by construction. The emission stops identically at the bevel, so the ground under the filename is bit-for-bit what it was -- qs-gpu's emission_never_reaches_the_middle_of_a_surface measures exactly that, because Material::composites checks the albedo and could never see it move. The shadow falls on the canvas, which rule 1a calls a receiver and lets take all the light. The halo still SWELLS while the selection travels, and the emission does not: a thing that got brighter as it moved would read as friction, where a spill that reaches further reads as speed. On the fallback tier the shadow and the halo and the rim all drop, the surface flattens to its albedo, and what is left is the plain selected fill the product always had.

$comment: THE SPILL: the light escaping from behind the row. Its reach is bounded by the
fill-rate guard rather than by taste — at 2xl the halo layer alone cost 3.58x the
viewport against 3.10x for the entire rest of the frame, which the row test
`the_halo_costs_a_measured_amount_of_overdraw_and_not_an_assumed_one` refuses by
name. `lg` is the largest step on the scale that passes it. The brightness (0.42,
up from a 0.1 whisper) is where the spill's presence actually comes from; reach
past `lg` buys area rather than presence, and pays for it in fill.
THE LAMP. Its albedo is the LIGHT'S colour, not the surface's, and that is the whole
difference between a lamp and a lighter rectangle: `shade_pbr` emits `albedo *
emission`, so a panel whose albedo is a dark blue-grey emits dark blue-grey however
far the strength is pushed -- it was authored that way and read as a washed-out fill
at every strength tried. With the accent as its albedo the same arithmetic emits
accent-coloured light.
The unlit form is unchanged in kind: with effects off this collapses to its flat stop
like every other enhanced layer. What the LIT gate checks is this albedo plus the
emission's closed-form peak -- see `Material::lit_composites` and `content/on-lit`.

chrome/bar.description: The command bar. The ramp catches light along its top edge and deepens into the hairline, which is what separates it from the list without claiming to float over it -- a drop shadow would say the two are different planes, and they are not. The hairline is a travelling SWEEP rather than a flat rule: an accent highlight circles it once per cycle, which is the one place in the window a moving light costs nothing at all. An edge band is excluded from Material::composites -- it is a hairline along one side, not a background -- and this band is genuinely one logical pixel tall with no text within reach of it, so the exclusion is honest here rather than convenient. It could not be authored until the bar was painted with a live drive: this call site pinned the drive at rest, so any phase on any chrome material was inert, and the sweep would have been a still line that merely looked slightly bluer at one end. The specular line on the top edge and the hairline on the bottom used to be a second and third Instance::rect pushed by chrome.rs immediately after the gradient, which is exactly the hand-built stack this replaces. THE HAIRLINE'S FAR STOP IS NOW AN EMISSIVE, which makes this band the only source the bloom's bright pass can select anywhere in the window -- see the $emissive_comment block. It was chosen for the sentence already three lines above this one: no text is within reach of it. TWO NUMBERS HAD TO MOVE WITH IT AND BOTH WERE MEASURED, NOT CHOSEN. The alpha went 0.85 -> 1.0 because a layer's alpha multiplies its stops, so an emissive arriving through an 0.85 layer lands below the threshold and the bloom switches off with a source authored, present and drawn. And the band went 1 -> 8, which is the honest cost of this chunk and the thing to argue with first: it is no longer a hairline. `--bloom-reach` swept it -- 1px changes 0 of 1,440,000 pixels, 4px changes 0, 6px changes 0, 8px changes 8,289 (0.58%, peak 10/255), 12px changes 21,396 (1.49%, peak 16/255). A bloom's blur is separable, so a source with one pixel of VERTICAL extent survives the downsample as nothing at all, however long it is; 8 is the smallest band on this bar that bleeds anything, and it is 8 rather than 12 because the design cost was minimised against the measurement rather than the effect being made as loud as it would go. What the same sweep says in the other direction is worth as much: the lift on row grounds is 0.0000 at every thickness tried, so the band's light stays in the bar and `content/tertiary over surface/row-selected` -- the tightest text in the product at 4.82:1, with 0.32 of headroom -- does not move at all.

chrome/chip-hover.description: A hovered Back/Up/breadcrumb chip. It was surface/row-hover at full opacity, which is a token authored for the ROW surfaces -- near-white in the light theme -- painted on a bar that is dark in both, under ink that is near-white in both: the label vanished on hover in the light theme and no gate could see it, because no declared pair covered that combination. The visibility now comes from the outline, which sits on the boundary rather than behind the label and so does not have to be paid for in contrast; the fill is only as strong as the dim ink can survive on the lifted stop. Between the two is the rim: a light that is brightest at the edge and gone two pixels inward, which is what makes the chip read as a lit surface rather than as a lighter rectangle with a line round it. It is the one enhanced layer here, so on the fallback tier the chip is its fill and its outline -- which is the plainer version of the same chip, and both of those already say it is hovered. Like the outline and unlike the fill, the rim is not counted in the composite the contrast gate checks, because it lights the edge rather than sitting behind the label; counting it was tried and the numbers refused it, since this chip has no headroom left over the lifted stop. The fill's 0.15 is still the number the dim ink has to survive, and it is why the rim is where the extra presence went.

chrome/shelf.description: The status shelf. Ramped the opposite way to the command bar so the two bookend the window rather than repeating each other, and its hairline sits on the edge it shares with the list. Its top hairline is a travelling sweep, like the command bar's and deliberately turning the OTHER WAY: the two bookend the window, and two lights circling in the same direction would read as one belt moving behind the list rather than as two edges catching it.

chrome/popover.description: A popover, and the inspector's panel: UXDD 10.2's 'depth via real blur'. The glass is surface/raised at 0.82 and the floor is the same token opaque, which is the whole encoding -- one colour, two roles, and the second is what a machine that cannot blur shows. The opacity is high because the gate says so rather than because glass is conservative: what sits under the label is the glass composited over the rest of the window, so the contrast check walks nine grounds from black to white and the label has to clear 4.5:1 on all of them. A showier 0.4 fails on the samples in the middle, which is the panel over a half-lit list -- the common case, not the exotic one.

$comment: Explicit, not inferred (data-model.md, Token). An inferred list either misses real
pairs or invents impossible ones, and both failure modes end with people ignoring
the gate.
`border/subtle` is deliberately absent. WCAG 1.4.11 scopes non-text contrast to
boundaries needed to *identify* a component. A row separator identifies nothing --
rows are already delimited by their content and spacing -- so holding it to 3:1
would force a heavy rule that makes a dense list harder to read, not easier. The
boundaries that do carry meaning (focus, status) are gated below.

contrast_pairs.$comment: The four overlay pairs that used to be written out here are gone, and their absence is the proof that the material expansion is real rather than additive. A gradient has two colours and text over it has to clear both, so the ramp is gated at the stop where the contrast is worst rather than at the one the token happens to be named after â€” for the command bar that is surface/overlay-lift, because the ink is near-white and the LIGHTER end is the harder one. `chrome/bar` and `chrome/shelf` now state their stops and their ink once, and the gate derives every combination, including the ones a hand-written list would not have thought of: the hovered chip's wash over each stop of the ramp beneath it, which is where the light theme's vanishing breadcrumb label was found.

ADR 013: the inspector's regions are grounded in surface/row-alt, and the focused region's 2 px accent edge is drawn over that ground. The pair existed on screen before it existed here, which is the failure mode the explicit list is meant to prevent -- an undeclared pair is not a passing pair, it is an unchecked one.

$comment: `directory-session-indicators`: the two outcome rails now appear on a FILE LIST
row, which they never did before -- they were the terminal pane's and the tab
strip's. A row's ground is not one colour: banding alternates surface/base and
surface/row-alt, the pointer adds surface/row-hover and selection replaces both
with surface/row-selected, so the rail sits on four grounds and the two that were
already declared were the two it did NOT acquire here.
border/subtle stays absent, and now for a second reason as well as the one above:
a live shell's rail is that token, so a folder whose sessions are all running
draws NO rail at all rather than an ungated one. The count in the size column is
what says the sessions are there; the rail is reserved for the two outcomes worth
interrupting for. See qs_ui::mark::SessionMark::new.
